title: Build your portfolio
desc: GitHub, pitch deck, and showcase prep
content_html:
What We're Doing

In this session, students take a project they have already built during the programme (a chatbot, a game, an image classifier, a website, or any other AI-powered creation) and turn it into a professional, shareable portfolio piece. They will publish their work on GitHub with a clear README, design a short pitch deck that explains their project to a non-technical audience, and rehearse a two-minute "showcase pitch" they could deliver at a demo day, to a potential employer, or to family and friends.

The goal is not to teach coding from scratch, but to teach presentation, documentation, and storytelling skills around AI work students have already produced. By the end of the session, every student should have a live GitHub repository link and a polished slide deck they can proudly share, plus practice explaining their project out loud in under two minutes.

Tools & Resources

  • GitHub – https://github.com — free account, unlimited public repositories. Students will need a working email address to sign up and verify.
  • GitHub Desktop (optional, for students not comfortable with command line) – https://desktop.github.com — free, no limits.
  • Gamma (AI pitch deck generator) – https://gamma.app — free tier gives limited monthly AI credits (roughly 400, enough for 1–2 full decks); once credits run out, editing manually is still free.
  • Google Slides – https://slides.google.com — free and unlimited; use as a backup if Gamma credits are exhausted or internet is unreliable.
  • ChatGPT (https://chat.openai.com) or Claude (https://claude.ai) – for drafting README text and pitch scripts. Free tiers have daily message caps and may occasionally require a wait when usage is high.
  • A phone or laptop with a camera/microphone, for optional demo video recording in the extension challenges.

Step-by-Step Activity

  1. Open with a 5-minute discussion: "Why do employers and universities look at GitHub profiles and pitch decks instead of just asking you to describe your project?" Capture 2–3 ideas on the board.
  2. Each student opens (or creates) a GitHub account at github.com. Have them set a professional username (not a nickname) and add a real profile photo or simple avatar.
  3. Students create a new public repository named after their project (e.g., swahili-chatbot, trash-sorter-ai). They upload their existing project files (code, images, notes) using the "Add file → Upload files" button on the repository page.
  4. Guide students to write a README.md file. Use this AI prompt as a starting point in ChatGPT or Claude: "I built a project called [PROJECT NAME]. It does [WHAT IT DOES] using [TOOLS/AI USED]. Write a clear, friendly GitHub README with sections: Project Title, Description, How It Works, Tools Used, What I Learned, and Future Improvements."
  5. Students review the AI-generated README critically — they must edit at least three sentences to make sure it sounds like their own voice and accurately describes what they actually built (not what the AI assumes).
  6. Students paste the finalised README into their repository's README.md file via GitHub's web editor, then commit the change with a clear message like "Add project README."
  7. Introduce the pitch deck. Explain the classic structure: Problem → Solution → How It Works → Demo/Screenshot → What I Learned → What's Next.
  8. Students open Gamma (or Google Slides) and use this prompt in Gamma's AI generator: "Create an 6-slide pitch deck for a project called [PROJECT NAME] that solves [PROBLEM] using AI. Include a title slide, problem slide, solution slide, how-it-works slide, results/demo slide, and a next-steps slide. Keep text short and use a clean, modern style."
  9. Students replace any placeholder or generic images with real screenshots of their own project (screenshots of their code, chatbot conversation, app screen, etc.).
  10. Students edit slide text to remove AI filler language and add specific numbers or details from their own project (e.g., "tested with 20 sample sentences" rather than "tested extensively").
  11. Pair up students. Each rehearses their two-minute pitch aloud to their partner using only the slide deck as a visual aid — no reading directly from slides.
  12. Partners give two pieces of feedback: one thing that was clear, one thing that could be clearer or shorter.
  13. Students revise their pitch based on feedback and do a final run-through, timed to under two minutes.
  14. Close with a mini-showcase: 3–4 volunteers present their pitch and GitHub link to the whole group.

Example Outputs

  • Chatbot project: A GitHub repo named kiswahili-helper-bot with a README describing the problem (helping students practice Swahili vocabulary), the tools used (a free chatbot builder plus a text dataset), and a "What I Learned" section mentioning prompt design challenges. The matching pitch deck has a title slide with a bot icon, a problem slide with a relatable classroom scenario, a screenshot of a real chat conversation, and a final slide listing two future features (voice input, more vocabulary categories).
  • Image classifier project: A repo called trash-sorter-ai with a README explaining how the model sorts recyclable vs non-recyclable items from photos, including a table of test accuracy results. The pitch deck includes a "before AI / after AI" comparison slide and a photo grid showing five example classifications, three correct and two incorrect, with an honest note about limitations.
  • Game project: A repo named ai-trivia-game including the game files and a README with clear "How to Play" instructions and credit to any AI tool used for generating trivia questions. The pitch deck opens with a bold problem statement ("Studying for exams is boring"), followed by a GIF or screenshot of gameplay, and ends with a roadmap slide proposing a leaderboard feature.

Facilitation Tips

  • Account creation (GitHub email verification, Gamma sign-up) can eat up time if internet is slow — have students create accounts a day before if possible, or budget an extra 10 minutes buffer at the start.
  • Some students will want to accept the AI-generated README or pitch deck text word-for-word. Actively circulate and ask "Is this really how you'd say it?" to push for personalisation — this is the core AI-literacy skill of the session, not a side task.
  • If Gamma's free credits run out mid-session, immediately redirect affected students to Google Slides with a manually adapted structure — keep a printed or projected copy of the 6-slide outline handy for this.
  • Watch pacing closely: GitHub setup tends to run long for first-time users. Set a visible timer for each major phase (GitHub: 30 min, deck: 40 min, rehearsal: 30 min) and give a 5-minute warning before each transition.
  • Pair students of mixed confidence levels for the rehearsal step — a more confident presenter paired with a stronger technical documenter often produces the best peer feedback.
  • If a student's original project is incomplete or was lost, let them build the portfolio pieces around whatever exists (even a partial idea) — the skill being taught is presentation, not perfection of the underlying project.
  • Some students may be shy about presenting to the whole group; make the final showcase opt-in and offer small-group presentation as an alternative.

Discussion Questions

  • What is the difference between a README file and a pitch deck — why might you need both?
  • When you asked an AI to write your README or pitch deck, what did it get right, and what did it get wrong or too generic?
  • Why is it important to use real screenshots and real numbers from your own project instead of AI-generated placeholder examples?
  • If a future employer or judge looked only at your GitHub repository, what would they be able to tell about you as a builder?
  • How is "pitching" a project to a person different from just describing it in writing — what does a live pitch let you do that a README can't?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Add a license file and one or two GitHub "badges" (e.g., "Made with Python", "Status: In Progress") to your repository to make it look more professional.
  • Medium: Record a 30–60 second screen or phone video demoing your project in action, upload it, and embed or link it in your README and pitch deck.
  • Hard: Deploy a live, clickable version of your project (using a free hosting tool suited to your project type) and add the live link to both your GitHub README and the final slide of your pitch deck, so anyone can try it themselves without installing anything.
